evidence.title: A Self-Tuning Minimal-Rule Fuzzy Logic Controller for High-Performance Induction Motor Drives.
evidence.abstract: This paper presents a self-tuning minimal-rule fuzzy logic controller for high-performance induction motor drives operating under field-oriented control. Unlike conventional full-rule fuzzy controllers and reduced-rule designs with fixed post-design scaling, the proposed method combines a fixed nine-rule Mamdani inference structure with a bounded online output gain adaptation mechanism. The nominal gain and adaptation sensitivity are determined offline using Particle Swarm Optimization, thereby retaining operating-condition responsiveness without requiring online optimization, rule reconstruction, or membership-function retuning. The closed-loop behavior is analyzed using a discrete-time Lyapunov framework derived from the induction motor mechanical dynamics under bounded disturbances. The controller is evaluated through fixed-step simulations incorporating measurement noise, 12-bit signal quantization, and a one-sample computational delay. Comparative results against a conventional PI controller and a classical 49-rule fuzzy controller show that the proposed scheme achieves a rise time of 0.15 s, a settling time of 0.26 s, a post-transient mean absolute tracking error of 4 RPM, negligible overshoot, and a torque ripple of approximately 0.44 Nm. Relative to the classical 49-rule FLC, the proposed design reduces the maximum number of fuzzy-rule evaluations per control update from 49 to 9, corresponding to an 81.6% reduction in structural fuzzy-inference complexity. The results indicate a favorable simulation-level trade-off between dynamic performance, disturbance rejection, and structural algorithmic simplicity. Generated-code SIL, Hardware-in-the-Loop testing, target-processor timing measurements, and experimental implementation remain necessary to establish practical embedded feasibility.

evidence.title: Harmonic content analysis of a soft starting variable frequency motor drive based on FPGA
evidence.abstract: As the demands for electric vehicles, electric aircrafts, unmanned aircraft systems, and other motor-driven systems increase, high-performance motor drives employing variable frequency control with higher efficiency and reliability are becoming increasingly important parts of the ever-changing technological landscape. This study proposes a Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA)-based variable frequency soft-starting motor drive for a three-phase induction motor. The inverter output voltage and the load currents are analyzed for the harmonic contents using MATLAB. In the experimental realization, a four-pole squirrel cage delta-connected induction motor is utilized with a switching frequency of 4 kHz. The current and voltage characteristics of the induction motor are studied under different operating conditions to study harmonic contents and the effect of changing soft-start duration. The findings demonstrate a low-cost, flexible control of the induction motor with improved harmonic performance.

evidence.title: Optimal Load Restoration in Active Distribution Networks Complying with Starting Transients of Induction Motors
evidence.abstract: Large horsepower induction motors play a critical role as industrial drives in production facilities. The operational safety of distribution networks during the starting transients of these motor loads is a critical concern for the operators. In this paper, an analytical and convex optimization model is derived representing the starting transients of the induction motor in a semi-static fashion. This model is used to find the optimal energization sequence of different loads (static and motor loads) following an outage in a distribution network. The optimization problem includes the optimal control of the converter-based DGs and autotransformers that are used for the induction motor starting. These models together with the semi-static model of the induction motor are integrated into a relaxed power flow formulation resulting in a Mixed-Integer Second Order Cone Programming (SOCP) problem. This formulation represents the transient operational limits that are imposed by different protection devices both in the motor side and network side. The functionality of the proposed optimization problem is evaluated in the case of a large-scale test study and under different simulation scenarios. The feasibility and accuracy of the optimization results are validated using I) off-line time-domain simulations, and II) a Power Hardware-In-the-Loop experiment.

evidence.title: Bifurcation and control of chaos in Induction motor drives
evidence.abstract: The induction motor controlled by Indirect Field Oriented Control (IFOC) is known to have high performance and better stability. This paper reports the dynamical behavior of an indirect field oriented control (IFOC) induction motor drive in the light of bifurcation theory. The speed of high performance induction motor drive is controlled by IFOC method. The knowledge of qualitative change of the behavior of the motor such as equilibrium points, limit cycles and chaos with the change of motor parameters and load torque are essential for proper control of the motor. This paper provides a numerical approach to understand better the dynamical behavior of an indirect field oriented control of a current-fed induction motor. The focus is on bifurcation analysis of the IFOC motor, with a particular emphasis on the change that affects the dynamics and stability under small variations of Proportional Integral controller (PI) parameters, load torque and k, the ratio of the rotor time constant and its estimate etc. Bifurcation diagrams are computed. This paper also attempts to discuss various types of the transition to chaos in the induction motor. The results of the obtained bifurcation simulations give useful guidelines for adjusting both motor model and PI controller parameters. It is also important to ensure desired operation of the motor when the motor shows chaotic behavior. Infinite numbers of unstable periodic orbits are embedded in a chaotic attractor. Any unstable periodic orbit can be stabilized by proper control algorithm. The delayed feedback control method to control chaos has been implemented in this system.

Firstly, it explains the origin, concept, key technology and application areas of digital twins, compares and analyzes the advantages and disadvantages of digital twin technology and traditional methods in the application of electric motor fault diagnosis, discusses in depth the key technology of digital twins in electric motor fault diagnosis, including data acquisition and processing, digital modeling, data analysis and mining, visualization technology, etc., and enumerates digital twin application examples in the fields of induction motors, permanent magnet synchronous motors, wind turbines and other motor fields. A concept of multi-phase synchronous generator fault diagnosis based on digital twins is given, and challenges and future development directions are discussed.

system.value: A Self-Tuning Minimal-Rule Fuzzy Logic Controller for High-Performance Induction Motor Drives.

abstract.value: This paper presents a self-tuning minimal-rule fuzzy logic controller for high-performance induction motor drives operating under field-oriented control. Unlike conventional full-rule fuzzy controllers and reduced-rule designs with fixed post-design scaling, the proposed method combines a fixed nine-rule Mamdani inference structure with a bounded online output gain adaptation mechanism. The nominal gain and adaptation sensitivity are determined offline using Particle Swarm Optimization, thereby retaining operating-condition responsiveness without requiring online optimization, rule reconstruction, or membership-function retuning. The closed-loop behavior is analyzed using a discrete-time Lyapunov framework derived from the induction motor mechanical dynamics under bounded disturbances. The controller is evaluated through fixed-step simulations incorporating measurement noise, 12-bit signal quantization, and a one-sample computational delay. Comparative results against a conventional PI controller and a classical 49-rule fuzzy controller show that the proposed scheme achieves a rise time of 0.15 s, a settling time of 0.26 s, a post-transient mean absolute tracking error of 4 RPM, negligible overshoot, and a torque ripple of approximately 0.44 Nm. Relative to the classical 49-rule FLC, the proposed design reduces the maximum number of fuzzy-rule evaluations per control update from 49 to 9, corresponding to an 81.6% reduction in structural fuzzy-inference complexity. The results indicate a favorable simulation-level trade-off between dynamic performance, disturbance rejection, and structural algorithmic simplicity. Generated-code SIL, Hardware-in-the-Loop testing, target-processor timing measurements, and experimental implementation remain necessary to establish practical embedded feasibility.

system.value: Harmonic content analysis of a soft starting variable frequency motor drive based on FPGA

abstract.value: As the demands for electric vehicles, electric aircrafts, unmanned aircraft systems, and other motor-driven systems increase, high-performance motor drives employing variable frequency control with higher efficiency and reliability are becoming increasingly important parts of the ever-changing technological landscape. This study proposes a Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA)-based variable frequency soft-starting motor drive for a three-phase induction motor. The inverter output voltage and the load currents are analyzed for the harmonic contents using MATLAB. In the experimental realization, a four-pole squirrel cage delta-connected induction motor is utilized with a switching frequency of 4 kHz. The current and voltage characteristics of the induction motor are studied under different operating conditions to study harmonic contents and the effect of changing soft-start duration. The findings demonstrate a low-cost, flexible control of the induction motor with improved harmonic performance.

system.value: Optimal Load Restoration in Active Distribution Networks Complying with Starting Transients of Induction Motors

abstract.value: Large horsepower induction motors play a critical role as industrial drives in production facilities. The operational safety of distribution networks during the starting transients of these motor loads is a critical concern for the operators. In this paper, an analytical and convex optimization model is derived representing the starting transients of the induction motor in a semi-static fashion. This model is used to find the optimal energization sequence of different loads (static and motor loads) following an outage in a distribution network. The optimization problem includes the optimal control of the converter-based DGs and autotransformers that are used for the induction motor starting. These models together with the semi-static model of the induction motor are integrated into a relaxed power flow formulation resulting in a Mixed-Integer Second Order Cone Programming (SOCP) problem. This formulation represents the transient operational limits that are imposed by different protection devices both in the motor side and network side. The functionality of the proposed optimization problem is evaluated in the case of a large-scale test study and under different simulation scenarios. The feasibility and accuracy of the optimization results are validated using I) off-line time-domain simulations, and II) a Power Hardware-In-the-Loop experiment.

system.value: Bifurcation and control of chaos in Induction motor drives

abstract.value: The induction motor controlled by Indirect Field Oriented Control (IFOC) is known to have high performance and better stability. This paper reports the dynamical behavior of an indirect field oriented control (IFOC) induction motor drive in the light of bifurcation theory. The speed of high performance induction motor drive is controlled by IFOC method. The knowledge of qualitative change of the behavior of the motor such as equilibrium points, limit cycles and chaos with the change of motor parameters and load torque are essential for proper control of the motor. This paper provides a numerical approach to understand better the dynamical behavior of an indirect field oriented control of a current-fed induction motor. The focus is on bifurcation analysis of the IFOC motor, with a particular emphasis on the change that affects the dynamics and stability under small variations of Proportional Integral controller (PI) parameters, load torque and k, the ratio of the rotor time constant and its estimate etc. Bifurcation diagrams are computed. This paper also attempts to discuss various types of the transition to chaos in the induction motor. The results of the obtained bifurcation simulations give useful guidelines for adjusting both motor model and PI controller parameters. It is also important to ensure desired operation of the motor when the motor shows chaotic behavior. Infinite numbers of unstable periodic orbits are embedded in a chaotic attractor. Any unstable periodic orbit can be stabilized by proper control algorithm. The delayed feedback control method to control chaos has been implemented in this system.

Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-023: A candidate that survives the 14-gate protocol at the CONCEPT level can be killed at the ELEMENT-DECOMPOSITION level. The 14 gates assessed M4 against the broad concept (continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface) and found M4=NOT FOUND. The combination is an aggregation of known anti-fouling approaches. The lesson: M4 must be assessed at the ELEMENT level, not the concept level. warnings.mechanism: Capability collision test — keyword collision search is insufficient to establish novelty
warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

informational.mechanism: RES-4 narrow: adaptive transverse/sigmoid sinus stent for CSF absorption regulation via AG pressure gradient control
informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. Control authority exists only in the stenotic+high-flow regime (D≤4mm, Q≥1200 mL/min), which is incompatible with a stented patient whose stent has normalized diameter to 7-10mm. The network model (1323 configs) confirms: flow redistribution through contralateral sinus does NOT rescue control authority (dominance has no effect). NOT a universal vascular invariant — based on Poiseuille model with specific assumptions about geometry, flow, and topology.

informational.mechanism: Minimum Sufficient Validation Evidence Derivation (MSVED) — 4-link chain: ML change → clinical pathway → risk envelope → minimum sufficient evidence → sufficiency proof
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.mechanism: Automated Sufficiency Proof Generator (CC-04 / MSES theorem) — formal proof that a specific evidence set E is sufficient to establish modification-specific clinical risk envelope R(Δ)
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

informational.mechanism: Non-Inferiority Statistical Engine (CC-08) — automated paired NI comparison with pre-registered margins for ML model modifications
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-021: Automating a standard statistical test (NI testing) for a regulatory context that explicitly requires it (PCCP) is NOT an invention. Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. The CEO corrected: high collision risk is a RED FLAG, not a reason to proceed. Kill immediately if the smallest surviving mechanism is standard statistics + ML context + automated reporting.

informational.mechanism: SGET (Strain-Gated Electrochemical Transduction) — A=strain pulse changes B=electrochemical sensor from 2D surface to 3D depth profiling. First synergy-2 candidate.
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

informational.mechanism: SC-05 Biofilm-Resistant Living-Surface Venous Interface — continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface with active surface-energy control at CSF-blood interface
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-023: A candidate that survives the 14-gate protocol at the CONCEPT level can be killed at the ELEMENT-DECOMPOSITION level. The 14 gates assessed M4 against the broad concept (continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface) and found M4=NOT FOUND. But deep collision revealed that each element (continuous renewal, dynamic topography, surface-energy modulation) is individually occupied by prior art. The combination is an aggregation of known anti-fouling approaches. The lesson: M4 must be assessed at the ELEMENT level, not the concept level. And M4=NOT FOUND means the search has not found comparable performance yet — not that it does not exist.

custody_records.raw_content: This paper presents a self-tuning minimal-rule fuzzy logic controller for high-performance induction motor drives operating under field-oriented control. Unlike conventional full-rule fuzzy controllers and reduced-rule designs with fixed post-design scaling, the proposed method combines a fixed nine-rule Mamdani inference structure with a bounded online output gain adaptation mechanism. The nominal gain and adaptation sensitivity are determined offline using Particle Swarm Optimization, thereby retaining operating-condition responsiveness without requiring online optimization, rule reconstruction, or membership-function retuning. The closed-loop behavior is analyzed using a discrete-time Lyapunov framework derived from the induction motor mechanical dynamics under bounded disturbances. The controller is evaluated through fixed-step simulations incorporating measurement noise, 12-bit signal quantization, and a one-sample computational delay. Comparative results against a conventional PI controller and a classical 49-rule fuzzy controller show that the proposed scheme achieves a rise time of 0.15 s, a settling time of 0.26 s, a post-transient mean absolute tracking error of 4 RPM, negligible overshoot, and a torque ripple of approximately 0.44 Nm. Relative to the classical 49-rule FLC, the proposed design reduces the maximum number of fuzzy-rule evaluations per control update from 49 to 9, corresponding to an 81.6% reduction in structural fuzzy-inference complexity. The results indicate a favorable simulation-level trade-off between dynamic performance, disturbance rejection, and structural algorithmic simplicity. Generated-code SIL, Hardware-in-the-Loop testing, target-processor timing measurements, and experimental implementation remain necessary to establish practical embedded feasibility.

custody_records.raw_content: As the demands for electric vehicles, electric aircrafts, unmanned aircraft systems, and other motor-driven systems increase, high-performance motor drives employing variable frequency control with higher efficiency and reliability are becoming increasingly important parts of the ever-changing technological landscape. This study proposes a Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA)-based variable frequency soft-starting motor drive for a three-phase induction motor. The inverter output voltage and the load currents are analyzed for the harmonic contents using MATLAB. In the experimental realization, a four-pole squirrel cage delta-connected induction motor is utilized with a switching frequency of 4 kHz. The current and voltage characteristics of the induction motor are studied under different operating conditions to study harmonic contents and the effect of changing soft-start duration. The findings demonstrate a low-cost, flexible control of the induction motor with improved harmonic performance.

custody_records.raw_content: Large horsepower induction motors play a critical role as industrial drives in production facilities. The operational safety of distribution networks during the starting transients of these motor loads is a critical concern for the operators. In this paper, an analytical and convex optimization model is derived representing the starting transients of the induction motor in a semi-static fashion. This model is used to find the optimal energization sequence of different loads (static and motor loads) following an outage in a distribution network. The optimization problem includes the optimal control of the converter-based DGs and autotransformers that are used for the induction motor starting. These models together with the semi-static model of the induction motor are integrated into a relaxed power flow formulation resulting in a Mixed-Integer Second Order Cone Programming (SOCP) problem. This formulation represents the transient operational limits that are imposed by different protection devices both in the motor side and network side. The functionality of the proposed optimization problem is evaluated in the case of a large-scale test study and under different simulation scenarios. The feasibility and accuracy of the optimization results are validated using I) off-line time-domain simulations, and II) a Power Hardware-In-the-Loop experiment.

custody_records.raw_content: The induction motor controlled by Indirect Field Oriented Control (IFOC) is known to have high performance and better stability. This paper reports the dynamical behavior of an indirect field oriented control (IFOC) induction motor drive in the light of bifurcation theory. The speed of high performance induction motor drive is controlled by IFOC method. The knowledge of qualitative change of the behavior of the motor such as equilibrium points, limit cycles and chaos with the change of motor parameters and load torque are essential for proper control of the motor. This paper provides a numerical approach to understand better the dynamical behavior of an indirect field oriented control of a current-fed induction motor. The focus is on bifurcation analysis of the IFOC motor, with a particular emphasis on the change that affects the dynamics and stability under small variations of Proportional Integral controller (PI) parameters, load torque and k, the ratio of the rotor time constant and its estimate etc. Bifurcation diagrams are computed. This paper also attempts to discuss various types of the transition to chaos in the induction motor. The results of the obtained bifurcation simulations give useful guidelines for adjusting both motor model and PI controller parameters. It is also important to ensure desired operation of the motor when the motor shows chaotic behavior. Infinite numbers of unstable periodic orbits are embedded in a chaotic attractor. Any unstable periodic orbit can be stabilized by proper control algorithm. The delayed feedback control method to control chaos has been implemented in this system.
